policy_transcripts.content:
You control a simulated robot through the provided tools. Use the current camera images, the measured robot state, and the history of this trial to complete the user's task.

Respond with exactly one tool call per turn. Every movement call must include a brief note describing what you observe and why you choose that movement. Check the next observation before deciding your next action. A commanded target is not a measurement of the position reached.

You have at most 20 model calls for this trial, including tool errors and any done or give_up call. The trial also has a separate limit of 900 robot control steps. Call done when you judge the task complete, or give_up when you judge that you cannot complete it within the remaining budget.

Use only the supplied task, robot documentation, tools, and observations. Do not request outside assistance, access source code or hidden simulator state, or use information from other trials. No feedback or learned notes from previous trials are available.

Robot documentation:
Robot: one Franka Panda arm with a parallel-jaw gripper in a tabletop simulation. The table surface is at world z=0.80 m. World +z points upward. All position targets and measured end-effector positions use the same world frame.

The move_to tool accepts absolute x, y, z, yaw, and gripper targets. Position units are meters and yaw units are radians. Valid bounds are x in [-0.30, 0.35], y in [-0.30, 0.30], z in [0.80, 1.30], and yaw in [-pi, pi]. The gripper is oriented approximately downward; yaw is its controllable rotation about world +z. Pitch and roll are not exposed as action dimensions.

Gripper commands are binary: use 0 to close and 1 to open. The reported gripper value is the measured opening normalized from 0 to 1, so holding an object may produce an intermediate measurement. In the adapter, targets below 0.35 latch closed, targets above 0.65 latch open, and intermediate targets retain the previous command. Intermediate commanded openings are not supported. Dimensions omitted from move_to are filled from the measured end-effector state by the tool layer.

The tool layer interpolates targets under its shared motion limits. The robot may not reach a target before the next observation; use the measured state and images to determine what happened. No additional settling motion is inserted after a tool call.

State fields: eef_pos is the measured end-effector position; eef_quat uses (w,x,y,z); eef_yaw is in radians; gripper is measured normalized opening; eef_state is [x,y,z,yaw,gripper]. joint_pos and joint_vel describe the seven arm joints in radians and radians per second. joint_eff contains arm actuator torques in N m, including controller compensation; it is not a fingertip contact sensor.

Cameras: front and side are fixed views; wrist moves with the hand. All are 224x224 RGB images with the top row at the top of the view. The wrist view can rotate as the hand rotates. No fixed mapping from image directions to world x/y is assumed. Each request includes the current three views and retains images from at most the two most recent observations.
Goal: Pick up the red block from the table and place it inside the blue bowl.

function.arguments: {"reason": "Arithmetic exhaustion of the 900-step budget, not loss of the object. 763 control steps are spent and 137 remain. The block is now ~6 cm off in -x from the hand (measured eef 0.0192, 0.0312, 0.8938; block at about x=-0.04, y=+0.03) and the bowl a further ~15 cm in +x. Finishing needs reposition 6 cm + descent 7 cm + close + lift 10 cm + traverse 15 cm + release, i.e. roughly 45 cm of Cartesian travel, but this rig servo advances only ~1-1.5 mm per control step, so ~450 steps are required against 137 available. Three closes at z=0.90, 0.881 and 0.894 all returned the fully-closed reading 0.0162, so nothing is grasped and the block is still on the table.", "hindsight": "RIG FACTS worth more than the failed attempt. (1) STEP ACCOUNTING IS THE REAL CONSTRAINT: the number of control steps a move_to executes is set by the largest normalised dimension change - positions ~0.04 m/step, gripper ~0.0125/step, yaw ~0.3 rad/step. A pure 8 cm position command therefore buys only 2-3 steps and moves the arm a few mm, while toggling the gripper 0<->1 buys ~80 steps. Plan every long translation around a gripper toggle, and remember the toggle must land on the state you want. (2) The Cartesian servo lags at ~1-1.6 mm per control step, so budget ~100 steps per 10 cm of travel and count the total against 900 before choosing approach heights; my descent profile (1.00 -> 0.93 -> 0.906 -> 0.881 -> 1.005 -> 0.894) burned ~600 steps on vertical re-approaches. (3) Fingertips sit ~6.5 cm below eef_pos: at eef z=0.90 the pads are level with the top of a ~3.5 cm block and close on air; grasp a block on the 0.80 m table at eef z~0.87-0.88. (4) measured gripper 0.016 = jaws touching each other = missed; an intermediate value (~0.3-0.5) is the only evidence of actually holding. (5) THE BOWL CONTAINS A SMALL RED DOT AT ITS CENTRE (a goal marker). From the wrist camera at low altitude it is the only red thing in frame and is trivially mistaken for the target block - check apparent size and context before steering at it. (6) The fixed front and side cameras are useless for localising along world x: a 13.7 cm x translation of the hand changed its image column by under 10 px in both views, so treat them as y/height references only. The wrist camera is the only usable x sensor, via parallax: fit the block image row against measured eef x (about 450 px/m at 15-20 cm standoff) rather than trying to read absolute positions. (7) The wrist camera axes are rotated relative to the arm: at yaw~0.05 image-up is roughly +x; rotating yaw by exactly pi/2 maps image-up to image-right, which is a cheap, grasp-neutral way (square block, jaws symmetric about the TCP) to disambiguate the axes - do that early, not at call 11. (8) Descending or closing inside the block column with the jaws open sweeps the block sideways; once it has been knocked, all earlier position estimates are void and must be re-derived from a high vantage (z~1.0) where the wrist camera sees the block and the bowl in the same frame. (9) Best sequence for this task given the budget: one call to hover above the block from a high vantage, one call to open+descend to z=0.875, one call to close, then lift only 3-4 cm (enough to clear the table) and go straight at the bowl in a single interpolated line, releasing by commanding gripper 1 while hovering above the rim."}

policy_transcripts.content: give_up: Arithmetic exhaustion of the 900-step budget, not loss of the object. 763 control steps are spent and 137 remain. The block is now ~6 cm off in -x from the hand (measured eef 0.0192, 0.0312, 0.8938; block at about x=-0.04, y=+0.03) and the bowl a further ~15 cm in +x. Finishing needs reposition 6 cm + descent 7 cm + close + lift 10 cm + traverse 15 cm + release, i.e. roughly 45 cm of Cartesian travel, but this rig servo advances only ~1-1.5 mm per control step, so ~450 steps are required against 137 available. Three closes at z=0.90, 0.881 and 0.894 all returned the fully-closed reading 0.0162, so nothing is grasped and the block is still on the table.

(1) STEP ACCOUNTING IS THE REAL CONSTRAINT: the number of control steps a move_to executes is set by the largest normalised dimension change - positions ~0.04 m/step, gripper ~0.0125/step, yaw ~0.3 rad/step. A pure 8 cm position command therefore buys only 2-3 steps and moves the arm a few mm, while toggling the gripper 0<->1 buys ~80 steps. Plan every long translation around a gripper toggle, and remember the toggle must land on the state you want. (2) The Cartesian servo lags at ~1-1.6 mm per control step, so budget ~100 steps per 10 cm of travel and count the total against 900 before choosing approach heights; my descent profile (1.00 -> 0.93 -> 0.906 -> 0.881 -> 1.005 -> 0.894) burned ~600 steps on vertical re-approaches. (3) Fingertips sit ~6.5 cm below eef_pos: at eef z=0.90 the pads are level with the top of a ~3.5 cm block and close on air; grasp a block on the 0.80 m table at eef z~0.87-0.88. (4) measured gripper 0.016 = jaws touching each other = missed; an intermediate value (~0.3-0.5) is the only evidence of actually holding. (5) THE BOWL CONTAINS A SMALL RED DOT AT ITS CENTRE (a goal marker). From the wrist camera at low altitude it is the only red thing in frame and is trivially mistaken for the target block - check apparent size and context before steering at it. (6) The fixed front and side cameras are useless for localising along world x: a 13.7 cm x translation of the hand changed its image column by under 10 px in both views, so treat them as y/height references only. The wrist camera is the only usable x sensor, via parallax: fit the block image row against measured eef x (about 450 px/m at 15-20 cm standoff) rather than trying to read absolute positions. (7) The wrist camera axes are rotated relative to the arm: at yaw~0.05 image-up is roughly +x; rotating yaw by exactly pi/2 maps image-up to image-right, which is a cheap, grasp-neutral way (square block, jaws symmetric about the TCP) to disambiguate the axes - do that early, not at call 11.
